Bourke Street MECCA Aesthetica About MECCA Since our beginnings in 1997, MECCA has redefined the beauty landscape in Australia and Aotearoa (New Zealand), leading in retail innovation and delivering the ultimate beauty experience. MECCA was created to demystify beauty – curating, celebrating and educating on the best moisturisers and must-have serums, latest makeup trends (and products) and scene-stealing fragrances. Our goal has remained the same since the beginning of our journey—to help our community look, feel, and be their best. After all, a lipstick is just a lipstick until that very first transformational swipe. With over 25 years of drive (and beauty obsession), MECCA has become Australia’s largest prestige beauty retailer under the leadership of our enterprising founder, Jo Horgan. Empowered by Jo’s gung-ho spirit, we now captivate over four million customers every year through our network of 100+ stores, our brimming digital content, ecommerce platform (and app!), and our best-in-class Beauty Loop loyalty program with an exclusive curation of over 200 of the best beauty brands in the world, and a high-touch, love-filled approach to customer experience. Empowered by Jo’s gung-ho spirit, we now captivate over four million customers every year through our network of 100+ stores, our brimming digital content, ecommerce platform (and app!), and our best-in-class Beauty Loop loyalty program with an exclusive curation of over 200 of the best beauty brands in the world, and a high-touch, love-filled approach to customer experience. It all started in the living room of Jo Horgan's Melbourne home, where she hatched a vision to search the world for the most exciting makeup, niche fragrances and cutting-edge skincare, bringing them home for Australians to enjoy. In 1997, the first MECCA Cosmetica store opened in South Yarra, offering an expertly curated selection of seven renowned global beauty brands, that weren’t previously available down under. By 2001, MECCA was leading the way with online shopping, enabling beauty enthusiasts to browse and buy their favourite products anytime, anywhere at our dot-com. Six years later, MECCA ventured across international waters to open its doors in Aotearoa (New Zealand). Beyond beauty retail, MECCA’s commitment to providing the best in beauty has extended into three brands: MECCA COSMETICA , launched in 2003 and thoughtfully crafted by beauty enthusiasts for beauty lovers; MECCA MAX – a collection of vibrant pigments and essential makeup and skincare for all – which emerged in 2017; and in 2022, kit: , a reimagining of the Kit: Cosmetics store concept that offers modern skincare and body care solutions made with premium, plant-derived ingredients and sustainable practices. We believe that beauty has the power to change lives. That's why in 2017, we launched our social change program, MECCA M-POWER , which aimed to assist 10,000 girls facing social and financial barriers to complete secondary school. Since achieving that goal in 2022, M-POWER now has a new mission: to create a world where women and girls can thrive and achieve their full potential – a world of possibility and opportunity, regardless of gender. Through M-POWER, we support a group of over 20 incredible organisations dedicated to creating a future where the next generation can thrive. We strive to fight for women by ensuring their access to education, improving their health, safety and well-being, empowering female-led businesses, supporting women to become financially secure and independent and elevating women's voices in politics and public life. Join us, and together we can make the world over.

Bourke Street MECCA Aesthetica Careers at MECCA With more than 100 stores, 200 brands and 7,000 team members, a lot has changed since our first Cosmetica store opened its doors in 1997, but our vision remains the same – to make every MECCA customer look and more importantly, feel and be their best every single day. Although we’ve grown, our entrepreneurial spirit remains strong. Everyone at MECCA is given the opportunity to influence, change the game and ignite their inner entrepreneur. We always strive to do better – for our business, for our team members and for our customers so we encourage our teams to create, innovate, drive change, and challenge the status quo. We take pride in all that we are and do Every time a customer interacts with us, we want them to have an exceptional experience. To do this, we need to look, feel and be our best, so that we can then help others do the same. We do whatever it takes We do whatever we can to hustle and innovate, if it’s in the best interest of the customer. title: Mecca draws bumper $110m dividend as revenue soars
body:
Mecca Brands has paid out a $110 million dividend after revenues surged to more than $1.4 billion last year, but the country’s biggest beauty retailer says the money has not gone to its billionaire owners but instead been funnelled into a special vehicle it will use for growth initiatives.

The figures were contained in new filings for the year to December 28, the first time that the privately owned retailing giant has provided a full account of its operations including its wholesale and distribution business.


Mecca opened a new flagship store earlier this year, a three-store complex in Melbourne. Arsineh Houspian

Mecca was founded by Jo Horgan, now the company’s co-chief executive with husband Peter Wetenhall, in 1997 and has grown even as rivals have struggled. The company makes twice the revenue from beauty as department store Myer, while its LVMH-owned competitor Sephora has found expansion in Australia more challenging than expected.

The accounts for Mecca’s parent company shows revenues rose to $1.37 billion in the 12 months, up from $1.29 billion in 2023. Profits slid marginally, from $128.6 million to $111.1 million, with higher leasing and wage costs.

The accounts show the company – which has one shareholder, a trust – paid $110 million in dividends. A company spokeswoman said on Wednesday that the dividends, however “did not go to the owners [Horgan and Wetenhall]. They go to a corporate entity that funds and invests in Mecca’s growth.”

The money, she added, had been partly used for the development of Mecca’s three-storey, 4000-square-metre flagship on Bourke St Mall, the opening of which was described by Horgan as “a profound moment for Mecca”. It has also been funnelled to its customer service campus in Richmond.

The Melbourne flagship store was originally set to open in late 2023 but was beset by delays, including protracted sign-offs from Heritage Victoria for the renovations needed for the site. Now that it is open, it has joined the revitalisation of what was once the city’s great shopping precinct, with the opening of JD Sports’ biggest store and Labubu retailer Pop Mart.

The company has plans to open 10 boutiques by the end of the year.

Horgan, who is the public face of the company, is bullish on bricks and mortar retail. On opening the Melbourne store, which is three times the size of Sydney’s flagship, Horgan said: “You can’t get your hair cut by a computer.”

Adore Beauty, an ASX-listed online competitor, has also begun opening its own stores and reported this week that there were early signs that the move was paying off with sales up almost 10 per cent on last year. It plans to operate more than 25 stores by 2027, a number which could rise to 50.

It is expected that the Melbourne store, which includes services such as ear-piercing, hairstyling and acupuncture, will be used as a blueprint for the refurbishment of other outlets across Mecca’s network.

The new accounts show the company has lent $43.6 million to related parties, up from $20.2 million one year earlier and $99 million in 2022. The last time Horgan and Wetenhall – who have a combined fortune of $1.25 billion, up more than 54 per cent in a year, according to the Financial Review Rich List – drew a dividend was in 2022 when Mecca paid $12 million.

Horgan and Wetenhall remain the sole shareholders of the company. In an interview with AFR Magazine in April, Horgan was adamant suggestions the pair could sell were pure speculation. “It’s not great fun [to read the rumours],” she said. “It’s nobody else’s business.”

Mecca’s profits stand in stark contrast to the performance of its competitor, French beauty giant Sephora. For the year to the end of 2023, Sephora, which operates fewer than 30 stores in Australia, posted revenue of $313 million, resulting in a loss of $13 million, according to its local filings.

title: Mecca, Chemist Warehouse, Priceline lead retail’s customer experience surge
body:
Retail brands have once again emerged as Australia’s strongest performers in customer experience, claiming nine of the top 10 positions in KPMG’s Customer Experience Excellence Report 2025/26, released today.

Specsavers topped the list, followed by Bendigo Bank — the only non-retail brand in the top 10 — and fellow optical retailer OPSM in third place.

The report draws on 80,000+ evaluations across 16 countries, including more than 5,000 responses from Australian consumers. Australia’s overall Customer Experience score rose to 7.30, up 1.67 points year-on-year, supported by strong improvement across the pillars of Empathy, Resolution and Expectations.

Beauty and wellness retailers remain some of the most consistently high-performing brands in the country.

Across the 2025, 2024, 2023 and 2021 reports, beauty retailers including Mecca, Chemist Warehouse and Priceline appear repeatedly in the top 10 — often outranking major supermarkets, tech giants and global e-commerce players.

Why beauty excels in CX
KPMG notes that Australia’s CX leaders are those combining technology, empathy and personalisation, with beauty retailers particularly strong in:

Seamless omnichannel journeys — Mecca’s digital-store integration continues to set a national standard.
High-touch in-store service — Beauty advisors delivering personalised recommendations and experiential retail.
Loyalty ecosystems — Chemist Warehouse and Priceline both leveraging member value to build long-term trust and repeat purchasing.
Agile, AI-enabled service models — Enhanced product discovery tools, personalised marketing and frictionless checkout experiences.

Carmen Bekker, Lead Partner, KPMG Customer.
Carmen Bekker, Lead Partner, KPMG Customer, said: “Retail and financial services are leading CX transformation, driven by omnichannel maturity, AI-powered journeys and loyalty ecosystems that reduce friction and deepen customer connection. Brands that excel are those embedding technology with empathy.”

Neil Shewan, Lead Partner for Experience Transformation, KPMG Customer, commented: “What will set organisations apart in the minds of the consumer is their willingness to embrace AI and innovation in addition to their ability to integrate customers, employees, data, technology, and operations into one coherent whole. At the same time, brands must continue to foster consumer trust and confidence. In the future, Australian consumers will increasingly rely on personal AI agents to filter information, make decisions and complete transactions. Brands must now create experiences that are engaging and trustworthy for people and optimised for the logic of AI agents, ensuring relevance and trust.”

title: Beauty Diary: Review of Mecca’s new $420 atelier ‘VIP experience’
body:
A glam squad is an experience only the incredibly wealthy can afford – but now, us mere mortals can get a taste of the high life, and it won’t blow out your entire budget.

Mecca’s newly opened flagship, located in the centre of the Bourke Street Mall in Melbourne, is not just a beauty superstore, packed to the brim with the crème de la crème of make-up and skincare.

The top floor of the three-storey paradise is also home to a series of different services, including the first ever Mecca Beauty Atelier, a place where you can book in for an A-list hair and make-up experience.

Think Kim Kardashian before literally every red carpet or on-screen moment, where you can have a full wash and blow-dry, gel manicure and an expertly applied face in just 90 minutes.

And while you might think it’s super expensive, a large chunk of the cost is actually redeemable against products in store, making it pretty affordable – particularly if you subscribe to “girl maths” like I do.

There’s a whole lot happening in this photo, including hair, make-up and a gel manicure. Picture: Instagram/BellaVarelis
There’s a whole lot happening in this photo, including hair, make-up and a gel manicure. Picture: Instagram/BellaVarelis
What to expect

There are a bunch of different options available, such as hair and make-up ($320) or even a make-up lesson to master using your own products ($200).

But I went for the VIP experience as I wanted to know how the other half live, even if it was just for one day.

The session costs $420, but $200 of that can be used in-store, which definitely takes the sting out.

Considering it also includes a blow-dry from one of the Josh Wood stylists – a leading UK hairdresser that has just opened its first Aussie salon in the new beauty superstore – it also feels pretty good value. After all, it’s not uncommon to pay $120 for a blow-out thesedays.

Once I checked in at the atelier, the stylist went through the look I wanted, before washing my hair at a basin.

Upon my return, my Mecca make-up artist greeted me, along with a nail tech from cult Melbourne manicurists, Trophy Wife.

This was where the magic happened. For the next hour and a half, my body was stretched into a variety of different shapes (think: human pretzel) as the three beauty experts worked together to get me spruced up and feeling my best in what felt like record-time.

Mecca's new atelier offers a range of services, including the $420 'VIP experience'. Picture: Rebekah Scanlan / Mecca
Mecca's new atelier offers a range of services, including the $420 'VIP experience'. Picture: Rebekah Scanlan / Mecca
It sounds expensive, but it includes a full wash and blow-out as well as $200 that is redeemable against in-store products. Picture: Rebekah Scanlan / news.com.au
It sounds expensive, but it includes a full wash and blow-out as well as $200 that is redeemable against in-store products. Picture: Rebekah Scanlan / news.com.au
‘Indulgent but efficient’

I’m not going to lie, I wasn’t sure it was possible, but it turns out, these guys had been in training for months to make sure they were up to the task.

“The Mecca team designed the service to be seamless and choreographed, just

like being backstage,” Maria Tsaousis, the brand’s chief new concepts officer, told news.com.au’s The Beauty Diary.

“Flexible stations allow multiple services to be performed in parallel, so nails, hair and makeup don’t happen in isolation, they flow together.

“The service was trialled extensively with internal talent and external collaborators until the formula was perfected: indulgent but efficient, luxurious but quick.”

I didn’t stop smiling, the staff were just so much fun to be around. Picture: Rebekah Scanlan / news.com.au
I didn’t stop smiling, the staff were just so much fun to be around. Picture: Rebekah Scanlan / news.com.au
Mecca’s founder, Jo Horgan, said she wanted guests to “feel like a celebrity”, after first experiencing the joy of a glam squad for herself while travelling overseas.

It took months of practice, and the rigorous testing of more than 250 services across global beauty capitals (London, Paris, New York, Hong Kong, LA and beyond), before Mecca was confident it had nailed the brief.

“The aim was to create a beauty ritual that feels indulgent and luxurious, but also efficient and accessible, perfectly in step with how people prepare for celebrations today,” said Ms Tsaousis.

“Customers love that they can walk out of the Atelier in under 90 minutes looking and feeling ready for the red carpet. The community element, whether it’s a bridal party, a birthday celebration, or just a midweek reset, has also been a hit.”

From this... Picture: Rebekah Scanlan / news.com.au
From this... Picture: Rebekah Scanlan / news.com.au
... to this. In 90 minutes. Picture: Rebekah Scanlan / news.com.au
... to this. In 90 minutes. Picture: Rebekah Scanlan / news.com.au
No detail goes unmissed

Indeed, when I sat in the chair recently, it was such a fun experience – I was laughing so much with the experts working on me, it almost felt like it was part of my night out.

It wasn’t just a joyful experience, but I felt like every minor detail had been considered, from the soft lighting that makes your skin glow, to the magnetic phone holder so you can film your transformation in real-time.

“The Atelier is more than a service; it’s designed to be a ritual,” Ms Tsaousis explained.

“With Café Mecca right next door serving up culinary icons such as LUNE’s pastries and Seven Seeds Coffee, the experience extends well beyond beauty.

“It’s a space of transformation, celebration and connection, where customers leave not only looking incredible but feeling it too.”

My only issue with it is the fact it’s currently only on offer in Melbourne.

Fingers crossed the service rolls out to some of Mecca’s other 110 stores across Australia and New Zealand soon, because as a Sydney girly, once you’ve had the VIP experience, it’s hard to go back.

FAQs
When are Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2025?
Black Friday 2025 falls on Friday, November 28 and Cyber Monday on December 1 in Australia. Basically, a long weekend of deals. Considered the biggest shopping event in the world, Black Friday sales are proving even more epic in 2025—so it’s time to start shopping!

What are the best sellers I should buy this Black Friday and Cyber Monday?
Let’s just start by saying this: there are going to be thousands of beauty products from many great sellers on sale this Black Friday and Cyber Monday. So, where to start? For us, it’s all about narrowing down exactly where you want to spend your savings on. Save on shipping costs by shopping from just one or two of the best retailers, so you can combine your shipping (which is hopefully free) and hold onto more of that hard-earned money. 

Australian beauty destination Adore Beauty is one of our favourite places to shop beauty. With brands at Adore Beauty like Clinique, Aesop, Dermalogica, Estée Lauder, M.A.C, Alpha-H (this sale is the perfect time to stock up in majorly trending products like the Alpha-H Liquid Gold treatment!) and It Cosmetics, the site has some of the biggest and best names in make-up and skincare. And they also sell sex toys, if you want to treat yourself. 

Equally as exciting, Sephora Australia has a huge array of beauty brands to stock up on Black Friday and Cyber Monday. From Rihanna’s Fenty Beauty to cult favourite Anastasia Beverly Hills, Sephora’s huge exclusive range will no doubt have something for you.

Favourite fashion retailer The Iconic also has a wide beauty range, and its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales are always worth shopping. With brands like Ultra Violette, Dyson and Napoleon Perdis, keep an eye out on The Iconic for the best deals on the day. Best of all, you can buy clothing and accessories and combine the shipping! 

And of course, Australian favourite Mecca (and Mecca Cosmetica) will no doubt have its own Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales—perfect for if you want to stock up on cult brands like Dr. Dennis Gross, Urban Decay or Drunk Elephant using Mecca discount codes. 

Which skincare brands have Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales?
Love skincare? Same. With literally millions (well, it seems like) of brands to choose from, it can be confusing to know what to invest in. So, how does one shop the best skincare deals this Black Friday? 

Some of our favourite brands, like SkinCeuticals, Alpha-H, The Ordinary and Medik8 almost never go on sale. But keep an eye on Adore Beauty in case their cult serums, moisturisers and cleansers are reduced over the Black Friday and Cyber Monday weekend. Likewise, Ole Henriksen, Biossance, Foreo and Murad all make some of the world’s most loved products, so check on Sephora’s skincare deals to pick up your favourite or discover a new product. 

Where to shop the best make-up deals this Black Friday and Cyber Monday
Need a top up of your favourite BB cream, foundation or eyebrow gel? Black Friday and Cyber Monday are the time to do it. Plan ahead if your favourite product is on sale and stock up for the months to come. Beauty is notoriously hard to get on sale, so your best bet is to stock up now. 

Make-up essentials from the likes of BeautyBlender and Zoeva are worth stocking up on (one can never have too many make-up sponges or brushes), as are staples like mascara and concealer. Brands like Benefit, L’Oreal and M.A.C will all likely be on sale, so choose what you want and have it ready in your wish list. 

It can also be a wonderful time to get across any new palettes or sets you’ve been wanting to try. Sets from the likes of Tarte, Fenty Beauty, Zoeva and Dior Beauty can all be found at Sephora. Mecca boasts sets from Morphe, Tarte and Stila, all staple pieces to have in your beauty cupboard. Again, start wish-listing!

When do Black Friday sales start for Mecca, Sephora and Adore Beauty?
Black Friday Sales start dates vary each year as well as retailer to retailer, but you can generally expect major sellers such as Mecca, Sephora and Adore Beauty to begin a few days, sometimes even weeks, before or around the official Black Friday date of November 28.

Last year, Sephora made their Black Friday sale offer valid from the evening of November 23 and Mecca’s Black Friday sales began around November 20, so we can likely expect something similar this year. Adore Beauty started their promotions on the official Black Friday date in 2024, and are likely to do the same again in 2025.

Tips for shopping beauty products online
Shopping for beauty products online can be a little intimidating, but it doesn’t have to be. There are real rewards to be found! If you’re hesitant, check out the product in store before November 28, so you know exactly what you want and ask for some free samples so you can test before you buy. Make sure you've selected the right shopping location (you’ll want to know the difference between the AU and NZ prices, for instance!). Otherwise, read reviews, check the terms and conditions, memorise when the offers and promotion valid dates are, and don’t be afraid to return—stores like Adore Beauty, Mecca and Sephora all have incredible return policies if a product isn’t right for you.

title: ‘Shame job’: Beauty influencer blasts Mecca over 50 cent makeup claim
body:
A beauty influencer has taken aim at one of Australia’s biggest beauty retailers, accusing them of misleading customers with a recent campaign.

This week, Jill Clark shared a five minute long video in which she branded Mecca’s new ‘50-Cent Face’ campaign a “shame job”, pointing out what she believed was false advertising from the beauty giant.

The campaign, launched in November last year, is aimed at highlighting the affordability of the retailer’s in-house brand, Mecca Max, and claims that, with a select few products, customers can achieve a full face of makeup for less than 50 cents per day.

The claim is based on the cost per wear of each of the products, which is based on a daily recommended usage amount.

However, Ms Clark claims there are some serious flaws with the campaign and she has decided to share them with her 144,000 followers on TikTok.

In the video, she questioned how exactly Mecca “quantified” its daily recommended usage amount, revealing she, with the help of Chat GPT, had run the numbers on some of the products used throughout the campaign.

First up was the brand’s Off Duty Serum Skin Tint, which sells for $32 for a 30ml bottle, with a cost per wear of $0.09, according to Mecca.

Ms Clark deduced that at this cost per wear price, it would mean there are 356 uses in the entire botte.

“Now, according to your disclaimer of this being based off daily recommended usage, for 356 uses in this bottle, that would equate to one single use being 0.084ml,” she said.

In the video, Ms Clark showed viewers how much 0.084ml was. Picture: jillie_clarkk/TikTok
In the video, Ms Clark showed viewers how much 0.084ml was. Picture: jillie_clarkk/TikTok
The influencer has called the Mecca campaign a ‘shame job’. Picture: jillie_clarkk/TikTok
The influencer has called the Mecca campaign a ‘shame job’. Picture: jillie_clarkk/TikTok
The influencer then used a 1ml syringe to demonstrate how much product Mecca is directing customers to use for their “full face”.

“The f***ed up part is not even the amount of product, it’s the fact that this has a six month expiration. Which means that at 356 uses, even if you wore this every single day, it would still expire before you had a chance to validate the 9 cent cost per wear,” Ms Clark said.

In a statement to news.com.au, Mecca claimed that all the products used in the campaign have a ‘period after opening date’ (PAO), which is “essentially a ‘best before’ date after opening - not an expiry date”.

“MECCA MAX’s PAO dates are conservative, and the expiry will depend on how the product is stored,” a Mecca Max spokesperson said.

According to an article posted on Mecca’s website in March, the POA indicates how many months after opening that the preservative system in the product will be able to fight off bacteria with maximum strength.

The preservative system doesn’t become immediately ineffective after this period, but it “might start to become a little bit less effective”.

As a general guide, the article states that any products that come close and have direct contact with your eyes, such as eyeliners and mascaras, shouldn’t be used for longer than three to six months.

Powders can be good for between one and two years and cream products, such as foundation and lipstick “tend to stay strong for up to two years”, depending on how they are packaged.









Influencer slams Mecca's 50 cent campaign
A beauty influencer has taken aim at...
more
In the video, Ms Clark also referenced Mecca Max’s Of Duty Blush Stick, with retails for $20 and has 6.5 grams of product.

At a cost per wear of $0.03, Ms Clark calculated it could be used 667 times before it ran out, with each use being 0.009g.

“That unit is so small that I can’t even show you what that looks like,” she said.

This product has a POA of 18 months, which is approximately 548 days.

Next up was the Whip Lash Tubing Mascara, priced at $26 for 8ml of products. At $0.26 per wear, Ms Clark estimated roughly 100 uses in the tube for 0.08ml of product for each application.

“Let’s be so for real, there is not a chance in hell you are getting one hundred uses out of this. This would be drier than the Sahara Desert if you tried to use it one hundred times,” she said.

“Mecca, I would really like you to show us exactly what 0.08ml of mascara looks like on the eyelashes.”

A Mecca Max spokesperson said that, in order to validate the measurements used for the campaign, six of the brand’s “internal product experts” were asked to create an everyday makeup look using some Mecca max products.

“We took their average usage amounts, measured on a precision scale (a weighing device that provides high level of accuracy when measuring minuscule amounts), and divided them by the product price,” the Mecca Max spokesperson said.

“We know everyone uses products differently depending on their preferences and skin type, which is why we took the average amount.”

Mecca has over 100 stores across Australia and New Zealand.
Mecca has over 100 stores across Australia and New Zealand.
The spokesperson said the Off Duty Blush Stick was used by each of the six product experts and the average weight came to 0.01g per use, which is just marginally above Ms Clark’s calculation. This is how the brand came up with the $0.03 per use figure.

In her video, Ms Clark also referenced some of content created by other influencers in conjunction with the 50 cent face campaign, claiming there are instances where appear to use significantly more product than the daily recommended usage amount outlined by Mecca.

“You greenlit content for this campaign that shows people using four to five times the amount of product than what actually validates your figures on this campaign. That’s false advertising,” she said.

A Mecca spokesperson confirmed to news.com.au that the brand engaged and paid influencers as part of the campaign, confirming that all of those creators who were paid were only wearing Mecca Max products in their content.

Mecca said the paid influencers were provided with the products, along with a cost breakdown to create their looks.

“One of the paid influencers even completed their own measurements using a micro-scale, to validate their 50-Cent Face,” the spokesperson said.

However, they noted that not all influencers had access to precise measurement tools, so the brand provided “general guidance” to help them create their makeup looks.

“This is why there may be some variance in coverage and may result in a very small difference to the cost of the look depending on how much of the products were used,” the spokesperson said.

Speaking to news.com.au, Ms Clark said she decided to look further into the campaign after being continuously sent and tagged in related content by her followers.

Ms Clark questioned why the Mecca campaign was greenlit. Picture: jillie_clarkk/TikTok
Ms Clark questioned why the Mecca campaign was greenlit. Picture: jillie_clarkk/TikTok
“The more I looked into it, the more I realised that there is actually a story here and there is something that does need to be told,” she said.

The beauty influencer said the initially issue she took with the move was that Mecca was releasing a price focused campaign in he cost of living crisis, but then she began noticing other details she found concerning.

She also confirmed to news.com.au that she is in a “non-exclusive agreement” in Sephora, one of Mecca’s biggest competitors.

However, Ms Clark said she doesn’t make money from promoting Sephora online, describing herself instead as an “affiliate” of the brand.

“So there’s no sort of obligations to post about Sephora. There’s no agreements in that respect,” she said.

In the video criticising the Mecca campaign, Ms Clark does not mention Sephora or compare the two brands in any way.

At the end of the clip, which has been viewed more than 600,000 times and received over 1700 comments, the beauty influencer questioned how the campaign was allowed to go ahead with the perceived issues highlighted in the video.

“It goes without saying that no brand, whether it’s makeup or clothing, can dictate to you your personal cost per wear, that is up to the consumer’s individual behaviour. And, as one of the biggest beauty retailers in the country, I would hazard a guess that you understand consumer behaviour quite well. So, how did this campaign get greenlit?” she asked.

“It’s like they think we are stupid. I hope as consumers this pisses you off just as much as it pisses me off.”

This is not the first time Ms Clark has called out the beauty retail giant.

Last year she made a TikTok video comparing Mecca Max products to name-brand alternatives and found they contained “literally half” the amount of product.

In one of her multiple examples in the video, she compared the Mecca Max brow pencil to the Anastasia Brow Wiz.

The former retails for $20 for 0.04g of product and the latter retails for $41 for 0.085g of product.

“Mecca Max is known for being the more affordable option. It’s not,” she said.

“Because that’s the same amount of dollars per gram, for a far superior formula.”

At the time, a Mecca spokeswoman told The Daily Telegraph that Ms Clark had been “quite selective” about the products she chose to compare.

She said some of the products featured in the video were more expensive because “we’ve chosen a superior formula and/or product packaging, which can increase the cost and therefore the price of a product”..
